<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:log}
For every $N\ge286$ and every admissible $A\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}$,
\[
\sum_{a\in A}\frac1a\le\frac12\log N+(\log\log N+2)^2 .
\]
Consequently an admissible set has upper logarithmic density at most $1/2$, and natural density at most $1/2$ whenever the latter exists.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
There is an absolute constant $\eta>0$ such that for all sufficiently large $N$, every admissible $A\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}$ satisfies $\lvert A\rvert<(1-\eta)N$. One may take $\eta=e^{-5000}$ for $N\ge e^{200000}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:lift}
Let $a\in A$ and $a=q_1\cdots q_t$ with positive rationals $q_j\ne1$ (repetitions allowed). If for each $j$ the $q_j$-pairs in $A$ contain a matching of size at least $2t$, then $A$ is not admissible.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Choose $(x_j,y_j)$, $y_j=q_jx_j$, for $j=1,\dots,t$ in turn from the matching of $q_j$, avoiding $a$ and all endpoints chosen earlier. At step $j$ there are $2j-1$ forbidden integers, each lying in at most one pair of a matching, so a pair is available. Then $a,x_1,y_1,\dots,x_t,y_t$ are distinct elements of $A$ and $a\prod x_j=\prod y_j$, with $t+1\ne t$ factors. (If $t=0$ then $a=1$, which is excluded by (P).)
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:paths}
Let $q>1$. Any $R$ distinct $q$-pairs contain a $q$-matching of size at least $R/2$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The graph with edges $\{x,qx\}$ has maximum degree $2$ and is acyclic (values increase along $x\mapsto qx$), so it is a union of paths; take alternate edges.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:packing}
Let $P$ be a finite set of primes and $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}$ such that every element of $S$ is divisible by some $p\in P$, and $x,px$ never both lie in $S$ for $p\in P$. Then $H(S)\le\frac12H_N+\frac12$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Fix $m$ and write $m=b\prod_{i\le r}p_i^{e_i}$ with $p_1,\dots,p_r$ the primes of $P$ dividing $m$ and $(b,\prod p_i)=1$. For each $c\mid b$ the divisors $c\prod p_i^{f_i}$, $0\le f_i\le e_i$, form a box $B=\prod\{0,\dots,e_i\}$; the exponent vectors of members of $S$ avoid $0$ and contain no two vectors differing by $1$ in one coordinate. Pair $B$ into adjacent pairs along a coordinate with $e_i$ odd if there is one; otherwise pair $B\setminus\{0\}$ along the first nonzero coordinate via $(1,2),(3,4),\dots$. Hence $\#\{d\mid m:d\in S\}\le\tau(m)/2$. Summing over $m\le N$ gives $\sum_{s\in S}\lfloor N/s\rfloor\le\frac12\sum_{d\le N}\lfloor N/d\rfloor$; writing $r_d=N/d-\lfloor N/d\rfloor\in[0,1)$,
\[
N H(S)\le\tfrac N2H_N+\tfrac12\Big(\sum_{s\in S}r_s-\sum_{d\notin S}r_d\Big)\le\tfrac N2H_N+\tfrac N2 .\qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $h=\lfloor \log_2N\rfloor$ and call a prime $p\le N$ \emph{bad} if $R_p<4h$; let $P$ be the (finite) set of bad primes. Every $a\in A$ has a bad prime factor, by the consequence of Lemma~\ref{lem:lift} noted above (for $a=p_1\cdots p_k$ with no bad factor, $k\le h$ and fresh pairs exist). Let $E=\{px:p\in P,\ x,px\in A\}$ and $S=A\setminus E$. Then $S$ satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:packing}, so $H(S)\le\frac12H_N+\frac12$, while
\[
H(E)\le\sum_{p\in P}\frac1p\sum_{x:\,x,px\in A}\frac1x\le H_{4h-1}\sum_{p\le N}\frac1p .
\]
By Rosser--Schoenfeld~\cite[Thm.~5]{RS62}, $\sum_{p\le N}1/p\le\log\log N+1$ for $N\ge286$; also $H_{4h-1}\le1+\log(4\log N/\log2)<\log\log N+3$ and $\frac12H_N+\frac12\le\frac12\log N+1$. With $\ell=\log\log N$ we get $H(A)\le\frac12\log N+1+(\ell+3)(\ell+1)=\frac12\log N+(\ell+2)^2$. The statements about densities follow by applying this to $A\cap[1,X]$ and, for natural density, by partial summation.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Harmonic mass is insensitive to $[N/K,N]$ (the interval $[N/\log N,N]$ has $(1-o(1))N$ elements but harmonic mass $\approx\log\log N$), so Theorem~\ref{thm:log} does not bear on question (ii).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:heavy}
$S\le3072\,\delta$. In particular $S+\eta<c_0/2$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $\omega(n)=\#\{p\in\mathcal{H}:p\mid n\}$. Averaging over $n\le N$, $\mathbb{E}\omega\ge S-\lvert \mathcal{H}\rvert/N$ and $\mathbb{E}\omega^2\le S+S^2$, so $\mathbb{E}(\omega-S)^2\le S+2S\lvert \mathcal{H}\rvert/N\le3S$. By Cauchy--Schwarz $\sum_{n\in E}\omega(n)\le DS+\sqrt{3DNS}$, whereas heaviness gives $\sum_{n\in E}\omega(n)=\sum_{p\in\mathcal{H}}\lvert E\cap p\mathbb{N}\rvert\ge NS/16$. Hence $(\frac1{16}-\delta)S\le\sqrt{3\delta S}$, i.e.\ $S\le3\delta/(\frac1{16}-\delta)^2\le3072\delta$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:smooth}
If $y\ge e^{200}$ and $y^{16}\le X\le y^{56}$, then at least $c_0X$ integers in $[X/2,X]$ are $y$-smooth.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $u=\log X/\log y$, $a=(u-1)/112$, $b=(u-\frac12)/112$, so $\frac18<a<b<\frac12$ and $b/a\ge\frac{111}{110}$. By~\cite[Thm.~5]{RS62}, $\lvert \sum_{p\le z}1/p-\log\log z-B_1\rvert\le1/\log^2z$ for $z\ge286$, whence the primes $\mathcal{I}$ in $(y^a,y^b]$ satisfy $\sum_{q\in\mathcal{I}}1/q\ge\log\frac{111}{110}-\frac{128}{200^2}>\frac1{200}$. For an ordered $112$-tuple from $\mathcal{I}$ with product $Q$ we have $X/y<Q\le X/\sqrt y$, and the $\ge X/(3Q)$ integers $r\in[X/(2Q),X/Q]$ give $y$-smooth $n=rQ\in[X/2,X]$. There are at least $\frac X3(\sum_{q\in\mathcal{I}}1/q)^{112}$ such representations, and each $n\le y^{56}$ has at most $448$ prime factors exceeding $y^{1/8}$, hence at most $448^{112}$ representations. So there are at least $X/(3\cdot89600^{112})>e^{-1400}X$ such $n$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:kQ}
Let $y\ge e^{200}$, $Q$ a set of primes $\le y$, and $z$ uniform in $[1,T]$. Then $\mathbb{P}(k_Q(z)>y^{40})\le\frac1{10}$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Chebyshev's bound $\vartheta(t)<3t$ (from $\prod_{n<p\le2n}p\mid\binom{2n}n$) and partial summation give $\sum_{q\le y}\frac{\log q}{q-1}\le3\log y+7\le4\log y$. Hence $\mathbb{E}\log k_Q(z)=\sum_{q\in Q}\sum_{j\ge1}(\log q)\lfloor T/q^j\rfloor/T\le4\log y$, and Markov's inequality gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:core}
Let $p$ be a non-heavy prime with $p_0<p\le P$, $y=p^{1/16}$, and $Q$ the set of non-heavy primes $\le y$. There are $Q$-smooth integers $k,m$ with $k\le y^{40}$ and $pk/2\le m<pk$ such that $pk/m$ is rich.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
For $Q$-smooth $k\le y^{40}$ let $\mathcal{M}_k$ be the set of $Q$-smooth $m\in[pk/2,pk]$. Since $y^{16}\le pk\le y^{56}$, Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth} gives $c_0pk$ $y$-smooth integers in $[pk/2,pk]$, of which at most $pkS$ are divisible by a heavy prime; by Lemma~\ref{lem:heavy}, $\lvert \mathcal{M}_k\rvert\ge\gamma pk$ with $\gamma=c_0/2$. As $p\notin Q$, $pk\notin\mathcal{M}_k$.

Let $T=\lfloor N/p\rfloor$ and let $z$ be uniform in $[1,T]$; write $z=ku$ with $k=k_Q(z)$. If $k\le y^{40}$, pick $m\in\mathcal{M}_k$ uniformly and form the pair $(mu,\,pku)=(mu,pz)$, both $\le N$. Failures:
(a) $k>y^{40}$, probability $\le\frac1{10}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:kQ};
(b) $pz\in E$, probability $<\frac{N/(16p)}{T}\le\frac18$ as $p$ is not heavy;
(c) $mu\in E$. Given $b=mu$, $m$ is the largest $Q$-smooth divisor of $b$ (as $u$ has no prime factor in $Q$), so $m$ and $u$ are determined by $b$, and $z=ku$ with $m/p\le k\le2m/p$. Hence
\[
\mathbb{P}(mu=b)\le\frac1{T\gamma p}\sum_{m/p\le k\le2m/p}\frac1k\le\frac{2}{T\gamma p}\le\frac4{\gamma N},
\]
and $\mathbb{P}(mu\in E)\le4\delta/\gamma\le8e^{-3600}<\frac18$.
So with probability $>\frac12$ both $mu$ and $pz$ lie in $A$. For $Q$-smooth $k\le y^{40}$ and $m\in\mathcal{M}_k$ let $s_{k,m}$ be the number of $u$ with $ku\le T$, $k_Q(ku)=k$, $mu\in A$ and $pku\in A$. The success probability equals $\frac1T\sum_k\frac1{\lvert \mathcal{M}_k\rvert}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_k}s_{k,m}\le\frac1T\sum_k\max_{m}s_{k,m}$, so $\sum_k\max_ms_{k,m}>T/2$; as there are at most $y^{40}$ values of $k$, some $(k,m)$ has $s_{k,m}\ge T/(2y^{40})\ge N/(4p^{7/2})\ge N^{57/64}/4$; the corresponding $(mu,pku)$ are distinct $(pk/m)$-pairs, and Lemma~\ref{lem:paths} shows that $pk/m$ is rich.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:words}
Every non-heavy prime $p\le P$ is a product of at most $16(\log p)^2$ rich rationals and inverses of rich rationals.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Induct on $p$. For $p\le p_0$ use Step 4. Otherwise take $k,m$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:core}; their prime factors are non-heavy and $\le p^{1/16}<p$. Concatenating the words of the prime factors, a $Q$-smooth $v$ has a word of length at most $16\sum_qv_q(v)(\log q)^2\le(\log p)\log v$. Writing $p=\frac{pk}m\cdot m\cdot k^{-1}$ and using $k\le p^{5/2}$, $m\le pk$, the length is at most $1+(\log p)(\log m+\log k)\le1+6(\log p)^2\le16(\log p)^2$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
